draft.title: Theories of conformity
card: Some studies test why people conform. Solomon Asch, a psychologist, ran experiments in the 1950s in the United States.

In Asch's experiments, a person was asked to match the length of a line to one of three lines. The answer was clear. The other people in the room, who were working with Asch, gave the same wrong answer before the person spoke.
Many people went along with the wrong answer at least once, even though they could see it was wrong. This shows that group pressure can push people to agree with a group that is mistaken.
Asch found that conformity fell when even one other person gave the correct answer. So the pressure is strong, but it can be weakened.
draft.remember: Asch showed that group pressure can lead people to agree with an answer they can see is wrong.

a.q: What did Asch's line experiments show about conformity?
opts: People may agree with a wrong group answer
People always trust their own eyes over a group
People conform only when the answer is unclear
People conform only when they fear a punishment
a.why: Many people gave the group's wrong answer even though the correct answer was clear. This shows group pressure can push people to agree. It does not show that people conform only when the answer is unclear, because here it was clear.
a.clue: The correct line was easy to see.

b.q: In a class test of Asch's method, Priya sees that the line is clearly 10 cm. Five classmates, who were told to, all say it is 14 cm. Priya then says 14 cm. Which explanation fits Asch's findings?
opts: Group pressure led her to agree with a wrong answer
She truly believed the group had measured it better
She was punished by a law for giving a different answer
She was making a protest against the rest of the group
b.why: Asch found that people may give the group's wrong answer even when they can see it is wrong. Priya's choice fits group pressure. Believing the group had measured better is tempting, but the line was clear to her, so that does not explain her answer.
b.clue: Priya could see the correct length for herself.

a.best: People may agree with a wrong group answer

b.best: Group pressure led her to agree with a wrong answer

problems.detail: The right option is the only hedged one ('may'). All three distractors use absolutes ('always', 'only', 'only'), so a test-wise student can pick the answer without knowing Asch's findings.
